common.Num: A number, or the NAME of a parameter as a string. `48` and `"hub_d"` are both valid; the string form is what makes the model parametric, and it is resolved against the document parameter table at build time.
common.PlaneSpec: Either "XY", "XZ" or "YZ", or an explicit plane {"origin":[x,y,z], "normal":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]} in world mm. In-plane Y is normal x xdir. FundaCAD is Z-UP.
common.region: A 3D point INSIDE the closed sketch area you mean, in world mm. A sketch with several closed areas (a ring, a plate with holes, two separate outlines) needs one point per area you want. Omit `regions` entirely to use the whole sketch.
common.operation:
How the new material joins what is already there (default "new"): "new" makes a separate body, "join" fuses into the target, "cut" subtracts from it, "intersect" keeps only the overlap.
Without `targets`, a join/cut/intersect acts on EVERY visible body the new shape overlaps, not just the nearest one. That is what someone dragging a face across two parts means; it is not what building a second part beside a first one means. Set `targets` whenever more than one body exists.
common.targets:
Optional list of body ids ["body1", ...] that a join/cut/intersect is allowed to touch. Bodies not named are left alone even where the new shape passes straight through them. Ignored when `operation` is "new". A join that names targets and reaches none of them is an error rather than a quietly-created extra body.
Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.
common.activeWhen:
Optional on EVERY feature type: a Num. While it resolves to 0 the build leaves the feature out, exactly as if it were suppressed; any other value, or no field at all, builds it. Point it at a parameter whose expression is the condition: param_set coreOn = "solidCore == 1", then "activeWhen": "coreOn". A NaN condition is an error, never read as off.
A feature that consumes a switched-off one fails and says so, so switch its consumers off with the same parameter. Skipping a body-creating feature renumbers every body after it, like suppress does.
common.MateConnector:
One side of a joint: a coordinate frame, an origin, a z axis that is the mating direction, and an optional x axis for rotational reference, named one of four ways:
  {"body":"body2", "face": <Selector>}   the face centre, its outward normal is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "edge": <Selector>}   the edge midpoint, its direction is the axis
  {"datum": <datumAxis or datumPlane id>}   follows that datum
  {"origin":[x,y,z], "zdir":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]}   an explicit world frame
A connector on geometry is a REFERENCE, re-resolved every rebuild, so the joint tracks the part as it changes. Set `body` whenever you use `face` or `edge`.

sketch.summary: A 2D profile on a plane. Makes no geometry by itself; extrude, revolve, sweep and loft consume it.

fields.entities: the curves, see the `sketchEntities` section of this schema
fields.planeId: optional; the id of a datumPlane feature, which is preferred over `plane`
fields.face: optional Selector; makes the sketch follow a body face
fields.constraints: optional; solved by the frontend, not needed for an authored sketch
fields.name: optional label

sketch.notes: Sketch coordinates are 2D IN THE PLANE. On XY they are (x, y); on XZ they are (x, z); on YZ they are (y, z). A profile to be extruded or revolved must CLOSE, the endpoints have to meet exactly, so write the same numbers, do not round differently.

extrude.summary: Push a sketch profile along the sketch plane normal.

fields.sketch: the id of a sketch feature
fields.distance: Num, signed; negative goes the other way
fields.symmetric: optional bool; sweeps `distance` BOTH ways off the sketch plane (the sign then means nothing). What a sketch on a datum plane inside a body wants

Positive narrows the far face (the way a part pulls out of a mould), negative widens it (an undercut). Must be between -89 and 89. Absent or 0 is a straight prism
fields.regions: optional; A 3D point INSIDE the closed sketch area you mean, in world mm. A sketch with several closed areas (a ring, a plate with holes, two separate outlines) needs one point per area you want. Omit `regions` entirely to use the whole sketch.

revolve.summary: Spin a sketch profile around an axis. With `pitch` it climbs as it turns, which is how a thread is made.

fields.sketch: the id of a sketch feature
fields.angle: Num, degrees. 360 is a full turn
fields.operation:

Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.
fields.pitch: optional Num, mm of climb per full turn. With a pitch, an `angle` over 360 means more than one turn: a 2mm pitch at 1080 degrees climbs 6mm over three turns. The SIGN is the direction of climb along the axis, and a thread that cuts nothing is usually a thread climbing away from the body: try the other sign. A field takes a number or a parameter NAME, so write -2 directly, or define a parameter whose expression is -pitch and name that. "-pitch" in the field itself is an expression and is refused.
fields.axisEdge: optional Selector naming a model edge to spin about; is preferred over `axis`
fields.regions: optional; A 3D point INSIDE the closed sketch area you mean, in world mm. A sketch with several closed areas (a ring, a plate with holes, two separate outlines) needs one point per area you want. Omit `regions` entirely to use the whole sketch.

revolve.notes: The profile must lie entirely on ONE side of the axis and must not cross it. For a thread, draw the tooth cross-section in a plane THROUGH the axis (XZ for a Z axis), set `pitch`, and wind `angle` to 360 * number_of_turns.

fields.sketches: list of sketch ids, in order
fields.profiles: alternative: [{"sketch": id, "region": [x,y,z]}, ...] to pick one area per sketch (a ring keeps its hole -> a tube)

fields.profile: optional Num in -1..1: 0 (or absent) is the circular fillet, -1 flattens it to a chamfer's chord, +1 pulls it into the corner

fillet.notes: A SEAM edge cannot be filleted, that is the edge where a face that wraps 360 degrees closes on itself, and the kernel needs two DIFFERENT faces to blend between. `inspect` marks those edges with "seam": true. The radius must also fit: it cannot exceed the smaller of the two faces meeting at the edge.

press-pull.summary: Push one or more faces along their own normals, or along the axis of the hole they end.

fields.distance: Num, signed: positive grows the body, negative cuts in
fields.operation: optional "join" or "cut", a label that must match the sign of `distance`. It does not change what the push does, `mode` does
fields.mode: optional "auto" (the default: move the face itself, as described in the notes), or "join", "cut", "new" or "intersect": sweep the face into a prism along its normal (along the axis with `direction` "axis") by `distance` and combine that prism with the body, or with `targets`
fields.upTo: optional Selector naming a target face to stop at, instead of using `distance`
fields.taper: optional Num, degrees. Leans a PLANAR push's walls as they travel (a moulded boss, an angled pocket); positive narrows the far end. Must be between -89 and 89. Ignored on a curved face and on an `upTo` push. Absent or 0 is a straight push
fields.direction: optional, "normal" (the default) or "axis". "axis" moves the face along the line the faces around it run along instead of along its own normal, so the cone, cap or flat floor at the end of a hole slides down the hole: negative makes the hole deeper, positive shallower, and the end keeps its shape where an offset along the normal would widen it. Every face bordering the pushed one must be a wall along that line, a cylinder parallel to it or a flat wall containing it, or the feature is refused. The line is a round wall's axis, else the face's own axis, else where two flat walls meet. `taper` is ignored with "axis"

press-pull.notes: A planar face extrudes into a prism and booleans. A cylinder, cone, sphere or torus is truly OFFSET, which is how a hole is resized. A freeform face that WRAPS (a full revolve, a swept tube) is thickened along its own surface; `inspect` marks those faces with "wraps": true.

shell.summary: Hollow a body to a wall thickness, optionally opening faces.

offsetFace.summary: Move faces along their normals without changing the rest.

draft.summary: Tilt faces by an angle about an axis (mould release).

hole.summary: Drill holes into a flat face along its normal: simple, counterbore, countersink, or a heat-set insert bore.

fields.face: Selector naming the flat face to drill into
fields.points: list of [x,y,z] hole centres in world mm, projected onto the face
fields.sketch: optional sketch id whose points (else circle centres) add positions; with no `face` the sketch plane gives the direction
fields.size: "M2", "M2.5", "M3", "M4", "M5", "M6", "M8" or "M10". Fills in every dimension below that is left out
fields.depth: Num, for a blind hole; defaults to twice the diameter without a size
fields.cbDiameter: Num, counterbore diameter (ISO 4762 socket head default)
fields.csDiameter: Num, countersink diameter at the face (ISO 10642 default)
fields.leadIn: Num, insert lead-in chamfer, default 0.5; 0 for none
fields.drillPoint: optional bool, a 118 degree cone at the bottom of a blind hole
fields.flip: optional bool, drill along the face normal instead of into it
fields.tapped: optional bool, a label only, no thread is modelled

hole.notes: Sizes are M2 to M10; a heat-set insert preset exists for M2 to M5 and is always blind. A through hole reaches past the far side of the body.

thicken.summary: Give a surface (or a set of faces) a thickness.

fields.targets:
Optional list of body ids ["body1", ...] that a join/cut/intersect is allowed to touch. Bodies not named are left alone even where the new shape passes straight through them. Ignored when `operation` is "new". A join that names targets and reaches none of them is an error rather than a quietly-created extra body.
Body ids are handed out AT BUILD TIME, so read them back from `build` or `inspect` rather than assuming them. Once built, a body keeps its id when other features are added, removed or switched off, and a join keeps the id of the body it merges into.

deleteFace.summary: Remove faces and heal the wound (defeature: takes a blend or a boss off).

cleanUp.summary: Merge faces that are pieces of one surface, drop slivers.

texture.summary: Emboss or engrave a pattern onto faces.

fields.see: the `texture` feature is UI-driven; author it from an existing document rather than from scratch

teardropHole.summary: Give sideways round holes a pointed or flat roof so they print without supports (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the roof leans from the build direction, 10 to 80, default 45
fields.flatHeight: optional Num, mm above the top of the hole where a flat roof sits, default 0

teardropHole.notes: Only removes material. A hole whose axis runs along the build direction is refused.

roofBridge.summary: Square off the top half of sideways round holes so the roof is a flat bridge (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.height: optional Num, mm the bridge sits above the top of the hole, default 0

counterboreBridge.summary: Cut the first layers above a counterbore floor into a slot then a square, so its ceiling bridges cleanly (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the flat floor of each counterbore
fields.layers: optional whole Num, 1 to 3, default 2 (3 adds an octagon layer)
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the slot turns about the bore, default 0

sacrificialLayer.summary: Close a round hole with a thin membrane to drill out after printing (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, a hole's inside face or the flat face it opens onto
fields.depth: optional Num, mm into the hole from its opening, default 0
fields.side: optional "bottom" or "top", which opening a picked hole face closes

threadRibs.summary: Turn a plain round hole into a self-tapping screw hole: thin axial ribs protrude inward for the screw to cut its own thread into (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the inside face of each hole
fields.coreDiameter: optional Num, mm, the tap/core diameter the ribs leave clear; 0 or absent defaults to 80% of the hole diameter
fields.startDepth: optional Num, mm the ribs start below the open end(s), default 0.5

threadRibs.notes: Only adds material, inside the hole. A hole running along the build direction is fine, unlike the roof tools.

zipTieChannel.summary: Cut a U-shaped channel under a flat face so a zip tie can loop through the part (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.faces: Selector or list, the flat face each channel is cut under
fields.insetDepth: optional Num, mm below the face, default 2
fields.span: optional Num, mm between the two openings, must exceed channelHeight, default 10
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees the channel turns on the face, default 0
fields.allowBreakthrough: optional bool, default false; without it a channel reaching the part's far side is refused

elephantFootChamfer.summary: Chamfer the bottom edges of a body touching the build plate, to cancel first-layer squish (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

elephantFootChamfer.notes: Finds the lowest planar face opposite the build direction and chamfers its outer edges. Edges the kernel refuses are skipped and reported rather than failing the feature; it only fails outright if none could be chamfered.

verticalFillet.summary: Fillet every edge of a body that runs parallel to the build direction (3D Printing Toolbox plugin).

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body
fields.onlyConvex: optional bool, default false; true skips reflex (concave) edges

verticalFillet.notes: Edges the kernel refuses are skipped and reported rather than failing the feature; it only fails outright if none could be filleted. A reflex edge ADDS material.

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

move.notes: All six fields are required. This is the ONLY way to place a primitive, since box/cylinder/sphere are always centred on the origin.

duplicate.summary: Copy bodies and place the copies, leaving the originals in place.

fields.bodies: optional list of body ids; absent = the active body

duplicate.notes: Like move, but the source bodies stay put and each copy becomes a new body. A zero transform still makes an independent copy.

joint.summary: Position one body against another by aligning a mate connector on each, and re-resolve those connectors every rebuild so the assembly follows the parts.

fields.moving: body id of the body to reposition; nothing else moves
fields.mate:
MateConnector on the MOVING body, the frame brought to meet `to`. One side of a joint: a coordinate frame, an origin, a z axis that is the mating direction, and an optional x axis for rotational reference, named one of four ways:
  {"body":"body2", "face": <Selector>}   the face centre, its outward normal is the axis
  {"body":"body2", "edge": <Selector>}   the edge midpoint, its direction is the axis
  {"datum": <datumAxis or datumPlane id>}   follows that datum
  {"origin":[x,y,z], "zdir":[x,y,z], "xdir":[x,y,z]}   an explicit world frame
A connector on geometry is a REFERENCE, re-resolved every rebuild, so the joint tracks the part as it changes. Set `body` whenever you use `face` or `edge`.
fields.to: MateConnector on the body it mates against, held fixed
fields.mode: "rigid", "revolute" or "slider": which freedom the joint leaves, so the UI offers the matching handle. The placement is the same for all three.
fields.flush: optional bool. Two mating faces meet FACE TO FACE by default (their outward normals opposed); `flush` points the connector axes the same way instead, so the parts sit on the same side.
fields.offset: optional Num, mm along the mate axis (a slider's freedom)
fields.angle: optional Num, degrees about the mate axis (a revolute's freedom)

joint.notes: Body ids are body1, body2, ... handed out at build time, so read them from `build` or `inspect`. A mate reference that no longer resolves (a removed datum, a face a change deleted) leaves the moving body exactly where it is and records a diagnostic, rather than failing the build or teleporting the part.

scale.summary: Scale bodies, uniformly or per axis.

mirror.summary: Mirror the active body across a world plane.

fields.tools: list of body ids applied to it

boolean.notes: Body ids are body1, body2, ..., NOT feature ids. Call `build` and read the body list before writing one.

imprint.summary: Divide a face into separate faces along a sketch drawn on it, adding and removing no material.

fields.sketch: id of a sketch drawn ON the face to divide
fields.body: optional body id; default the body owning the sketch's face

imprint.notes: The curves must reach the face's edges to cut off a region; ones that don't leave the face whole and report an advisory. Each new face can then be pressed, painted or offset on its own.

datumPlane.summary: A construction plane other features can sit on.

fields.plane: PlaneSpec, the reference; with `planeId` or `face` it is only the cache used when that reference stops resolving
fields.planeId: optional id of another datumPlane feature above this one, which is preferred over `plane`: this plane then follows it
fields.face: optional Selector to follow a body face
fields.at: optional [x,y,z] pick point, needed on a round face
fields.offset: optional Num, mm along the reference normal
fields.shiftX: optional Num, mm along the reference x axis, moves the point the tilts turn about
fields.shiftY: optional Num, mm along the reference y axis
fields.tiltX: optional Num, degrees about the reference x axis through the shifted point, right handed
fields.tiltY: optional Num, degrees about the y axis as tiltX left it
fields.spin: optional Num, degrees about the normal as both tilts left it, turns the plane's own x and y
fields.name: optional label

datumPlane.notes: Placement is reference frame, then shiftX/shiftY/offset along the reference's own axes, then tiltX, tiltY and spin in that order about the resulting point. Every number is relative to the reference, so the plane follows its parent datum or face and every value can be a parameter name. A plane 20 mm above XY leaning 30 degrees: {"plane":"XY", "offset":20, "tiltX":30}.

datumPoint.summary: A reference point in space, a marker with no geometry that other features and the user can snap to.

datumAxis.summary: A reference axis, an infinite construction line other features (revolve, circular pattern, mirror, a joint) can be aimed at by name.

fields.dir: [x,y,z], its direction; need not be unit length
fields.axisEdge: optional Selector anchoring the axis to a straight model EDGE; the engine re-resolves that edge every rebuild so the axis FOLLOWS the part, and origin/dir stay as the cache it falls back to
fields.name: optional label

import.summary: A body read from a geometry file. Use the `doc_import` TOOL, never feature_add: `geom` is a content hash in the blob store, and only the import itself can put the geometry there, so a hand-written one names a blob that does not exist.

fields.name: label
fields.geom: content hash in the document blob store
fields.source: the file it was read from, for reference
fields.solid: Bool, false means a surface body that cannot be cut

import.notes: The tool takes `path` when the file is one this machine can open, or `content` (the file itself, base64, with `name`) when you are holding the file and your host will not give you a path to it. A text format can go as it is with encoding "text". Inline, gzip it first: STEP is text and shrinks about tenfold, which is the difference between one message and ten. Still too big? Encode the WHOLE file once, split the text that comes out, and send the pieces with `part` and `parts`, quoting the `upload` id the first reply gives back. Do not encode each piece separately, the halves of a base64 string join back up and separately encoded pieces do not. Remember that content is written by YOU: every piece is a message of your own output, so past a handful of pieces the answer is to ask for a path rather than to keep typing. An imported body is ordinary geometry once it is in: `inspect` gives its faces and edges with selectors, and it can be cut, filleted and measured against like anything else. `solid: false` means the file did not close into a watertight solid, so a boolean against it will disappoint: say so rather than press on.

arc.mx: Num, a point ON the arc between the ends

spline.points: [{x, y}, ...], the curve passes through every point

bspline.poles: [{x, y}, ...] control points: the curve is pulled toward them and passes only through the two end poles of an open curve
bspline.degree: 2, 3 or 5 (default 3), lowered to one less than the pole count when there are fewer poles
bspline.closed: true for a smooth closed loop (3 or more poles), which is a profile on its own
bspline.knots: optional, written by the app when a pole is inserted; leave it out for evenly spaced knots

sketchNotes:
Every entity may carry an `id` (unique within the sketch) and `construction: true`, which draws it without letting it bound a profile.
A profile that will be extruded or revolved must be CLOSED: consecutive endpoints must be numerically identical, not merely close.
A sketch drawn on XZ has its 2D x along world X and its 2D y along world Z.
howTo:
Working order that avoids most dead ends:

1. `param_set` the driving dimensions FIRST, then write features that reference
   them by name. Retrofitting parameters means rewriting every feature.
2. `feature_add` a few features, then `build`. Build often: an error names the
   feature that caused it, and one at a time is far easier to place than six.
3. `inspect` after a build to learn the body ids, the face and edge lists, and
   the ready-made selectors. Never guess a selector.
4. `view` to look at it. Numbers say a hole is 8mm across; only the picture says
   it is in the wrong place.
5. `doc_save` to a .funda file, which the app opens directly.

Asked to fit something to a part that exists as a file (STEP, STL, 3MF, OBJ,
BREP, GLB)? `doc_import` it first, then `build` and `inspect` it: that gives the
real sizes and the selectors for its faces and edges, which is what makes the
next feature something other than a guess. Import once and keep the document, a
large STEP is minutes of reading. If the file was given to you rather than left
on this machine, send it as `content` and skip looking for a path that is not
there: gzipped, and in pieces if it is still too big for one message.

If it is too big for even that, the answer is never to model against a
simplified stand-in you made up. A part fitted to an approximation of the
reference is wrong in a way nothing downstream can detect, because every
measurement you take afterwards agrees with every other one. Ask instead. The
person you are working with is at the machine FundaCAD is running on: they can
give you the file's path there, or open it themselves with File, Import Mesh,
after which it is in the document and `inspect` measures the real thing. Saying
"I cannot reach this file, what is its path on your machine?" costs one message
and gets the actual part.

Things that are true here and not in every CAD:
 - Z is up. A sketch on XY is a floor plan; a sketch on XZ is a side elevation.
 - box, cylinder and sphere are CENTRED ON THE ORIGIN. Use `move` to place them.
 - Body ids (body1, body2, ...) are handed out at build time and are NOT feature
   ids. Read them from `build` or `inspect`. A body keeps its id afterwards.
 - A feature can only reference features ABOVE it in the timeline.
